summary: This article presents a rigorous case study investigating five closed GitHub issues concerning session-isolation defects in major LLM agent frameworks and memory libraries. By systematically re-running historical versions against deterministic stubs and synthetic canaries, the author demonstrates that three issues reproduced and were fixed, one was a misdiagnosis involving a race condition, and one did not reproduce.
strengths: Rigorous methodology involving historical version pinning and deterministic reproduction scripts.
Brings practical, hands-on empirical value to developers by checking whether reported security/isolation bugs actually reproduce.
Clearly structured with actionable lessons for automated issue mining studies.
Demonstrates exceptional diligence by testing across multiple dependency versions.
weaknesses: No supporting code repository is publicly provided with the submission, restricting independent verification to manual script execution from the text path descriptions.
Convenience sample size is small (n=5), though appropriately framed as a case study illustration.
suggestions: Publish the mentioned reproduction scripts in a public GitHub repository to elevate the submission to a verified_open badge.
Expand the sample size in future work to validate the hypotheses proposed for the broader mining study.

claims.text: mem0 #6277: metadata in update() overwrote user_id, reproduced on 2.0.12 and fixed in 2.0.13
Agno #9319: per-user entity memory keyed without the user, reproduced on 2.8.6 and fixed in 3.0.0
LlamaIndex #21774: AgentWorkflow state leaked between runs, reproduced on 0.14.19 and fixed in 0.14.23

novelty_vs_existing.title: Where Agent Frameworks Fall Short: Examining Functional Challenges and Usability Concerns
novelty_vs_existing.contribution: Focuses specifically on validating reproducibility of closed session-isolation bug reports through deterministic stubs and canary tests, whereas existing literature covers broad bug taxonomies.
